q-12496.solution:
In this case, the ${x}^{3}$ that's outside the parentheses isn't quite the derivative of $(@@BASE@@).$ But the derivative is $4{x}^{3},$ so we're only out by a constant factor. 

So we make the substitution

$$
u=@@BASE@@.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =4{x}^{3}\,⟹\,\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u={x}^{3}\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and we can now write our integral in terms of $u,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{3}{(@@BASE@@)}^{9}\,\text{d}x & =\int (@@BASE@@)^{9}\cdot {x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {u}^{9}\cdot \frac{1}{4}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int {u}^{9}\,\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}\int {u}^{9}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{{u}^{10}}{10}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{40}{u}^{10}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{40}(@@BASE@@)^{10}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

q-113710.solution:
In this case, the term $2{x}^{5}$ outside the parentheses isn't quite the derivative of $@@BASE@@.$ But the derivative is $6{x}^{5},$ so we're only out by a constant factor.
So we make the substitution

$$
u=@@BASE@@.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =6{x}^{5}\,⟹\,\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u=2{x}^{5}\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and we can now write our integral in terms of $u,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2{x}^{5}(@@BASE@@)^{5}\,\text{d}x & =\int (@@BASE@@)^{5}\cdot 2{x}^{5}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {u}^{5}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int {u}^{5}\,\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}\int {u}^{5}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{{u}^{6}}{6}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{18}{u}^{6}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{18}(@@BASE@@)^{6}+C \\  & =\frac{(@@BASE@@)^{6}}{18}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

q-113715.solution:
In this case, the $2{x}^{2}$ that's outside the square root isn't quite the derivative of $@@BASE@@.$ But the derivative is $3{x}^{2},$ so we're only out by a constant factor.

So we make the substitution

$$
u=@@BASE@@.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =3{x}^{2}\,⟹\,\frac{2}{3}\text{d}u=2{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and we can now write our integral in terms of $u,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2{x}^{2}\sqrt{@@BASE@@}\,\text{d}x & =\int \sqrt{@@BASE@@}\cdot 2{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{2}{3}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\int {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}\int {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{2}{3}\cdot \frac{{u}^{3/2}}{(\frac{3}{2})}+C \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\cdot \frac{2}{3}\cdot {u}^{3/2} \\  & =\frac{4}{9}{u}^{3/2}+C \\  & =\frac{4}{9}\sqrt{{u}^{3}}+C \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{(@@BASE@@)^{3}}}{9}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

q-2379.solution:
In this case, the $x$ that's outside the parentheses isn't quite the derivative of $(@@BASE@@).$ But the derivative is $-2x,$ so we're only out by a constant factor. 

So we make the substitution

$$
u=@@BASE@@.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =-2x\,⟹\,(-\frac{1}{2})\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and we can now write our integral in terms of $u,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x{(@@BASE@@)}^{5}\,\text{d}x & =\int {(@@BASE@@)}^{5}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {u}^{5}\cdot (-\frac{1}{2})\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\int {u}^{5}\,\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}\int {u}^{5}\,\text{d}u & =-\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{{u}^{6}}{6}+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{12}{u}^{6}+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{12}{(@@BASE@@)}^{6}+C \\  & =-\frac{{(@@BASE@@)}^{6}}{12}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

q-72467.solution:
In this case, the $x$ that's outside the square root isn't quite the derivative of $(@@BASE@@).$ But the derivative is $2x,$ so we're only out by a constant factor.

So we make the substitution

$$
u=@@BASE@@.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =2x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and we can now write our integral in terms of $u,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x\sqrt{@@BASE@@}\,\text{d}x & =\int \sqrt{@@BASE@@}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\int {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{{u}^{3/2}}{(\frac{3}{2})}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{2}{3}\cdot {u}^{3/2}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{u}^{3/2}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\sqrt{{u}^{3}}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\sqrt{(@@BASE@@)^{3}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$
